content: The University of Kansas, commonly referred to as KU or Kansas, is a higher education institution located in Lawrence, Kansas. Its main campus is situated on Mount Oread. The university was established in 1865 by the citizens of Lawrence under a charter from the Kansas Legislature. Significant contributions to its founding included a donation of 40 acres of land on Mount Oread by former Kansas Governor Charles Robinson and his wife Sara, as well as substantial monetary donations from philanthropist Amos Adams Lawrence. The University of Kansas Medical Center and Hospital are located in Kansas City, Kansas. Additionally, the KU Edwards Campus is situated in Overland Park, Kansas, within the Kansas City metropolitan area. The university also operates educational and research facilities in Parsons and Topeka, as well as a branch of the KU School of Medicine in Wichita. As of the most recent enrollment data, the Lawrence and Edwards campuses collectively host 27,875 students, while the KU Medical Center enrolls an additional 2,769 students, bringing the total university enrollment to 30,644 across all campuses. The Lawrence campus and the KU Medical Center together employ 2,201 faculty members. KU is home to several notable institutions, including the Robert J. Dole Institute of Politics, the Beach Center on Disability, and two radio stations: KANU and KJHK. KANU, known as Kansas Public Radio, was one of the first public radio stations in the United States. KJHK, the campus radio station, has been student-run since its inception in 1952. The university also houses prominent museums, such as the KU Natural History Museum, the KU Museum of Anthropology, and the Spencer Museum of Art. The University of Kansas is a member of the prestigious Association of American Universities, which includes only 60 institutions. The current chancellor, Robert Hemenway, has held the position since 1995 and has actively worked to enhance the university's academic standing. Academically, KU is a large state-sponsored university with a diverse range of schools, including those dedicated to Allied Health, Architecture and Urban Design, Business, Education, Engineering, Fine Arts, Journalism and Mass Communication, Law, Medicine, Nursing, Pharmacy, and Social Welfare. The university also offers a selective Honors Program, admitting approximately 300 undergraduate students annually. KU has been recognized as one of America’s premier universities by Peterson’s Guide to Competitive Colleges and has received a four-star rating from The Fiske Guide to Colleges for academics, social life, and overall quality of university life. U.S. News & World Report ranks KU among the top national universities and public universities in the United States. The KU Medical Center in Kansas City, Kansas, treats over 19,000 patients annually and comprises four schools: the KU School of Medicine, the School of Nursing, the School of Allied Health, and a second School of Graduate Studies. As of Spring 2007, 2,769 students were enrolled at KU Med. Thirdand fourth-year medical students have the opportunity to complete rotations at the Wichita campus. The KU Edwards Campus, established in 1993 in Overland Park, Kansas, focuses on providing adults with opportunities to complete college degrees. Approximately 2,100 students, with an average age of 32, attend the Edwards Campus. Programs offered include developmental psychology, public administration, social work, systems analysis, and engineering management. KU has a rich history of innovation in computing. Its School of Business launched interdisciplinary management science graduate studies in operations research in 1965, which supported NASA’s Apollo Command Capsule Recovery Operations. KU’s academic computing department played a significant role in the development of the Internet and created the Lynx text-based web browser, which enabled hypertext browsing and navigation before the advent of HTTP and HTML. The university’s sports teams, known as the Jayhawks, wear crimson and royal blue and compete in NCAA Division I athletics as part of the Big 12 Conference. KU has won nine NCAA National Championships across various sports, including men’s basketball, indoor and outdoor track and field, and cross country. The football team, established in 1890, has participated in the Orange Bowl three times and plays at the historic Memorial Stadium, which is undergoing renovations to include a $30 million football practice facility. The men’s basketball team, a perennial national contender, plays at Allen Fieldhouse and has a storied history, including coaches such as Dr. James Naismith, the inventor of basketball, and Phog Allen, known as the Father of Basketball Coaching. KU’s student newspaper, The University Daily Kansan, has received national recognition, including first place in the Intercollegiate Writing Competition of the William Randolph Hearst Writing Foundation. The KU Department of English publishes the Coal City Review, an annual literary journal featuring prose, poetry, and illustrations. The university boasts a distinguished list of alumni, including Nobel laureates, prominent politicians, business leaders, and renowned figures in the arts and sciences. Notable alumni include Vernon L. Smith, recipient of the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences; Bob Dole, former U.S. Senate Majority Leader and presidential candidate; and Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto. KU is consistently recognized as one of the best value institutions in higher education by publications such as Kiplinger’s and The Princeton Review. Its tuition rates are below the national average, and the university offers a Four-Year Tuition Compact, ensuring fixed tuition rates for first-time freshmen for 48 months.
